25 A man standing next to a stationary train hears sound of frequency 400 Hz emitted from the
train’s horn. The train then moves directly away from the man and sounds its horn when it has a
speed of 50 m s–1. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s–1.
What is the difference in frequency of the sound heard by the man on the two occasions?
A
51 Hz
B
69 Hz
C
350 Hz
D
470 Hz

hints: Notice the first $400 \text{ Hz}$ is heard with the train stationary, so it is the source frequency, while the second hearing is with the $50 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ train moving directly away.
For a receding source the wavefronts are stretched, so use observed frequency $f_o = f_s v/(v + v_s)$ with $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Calculate $340/(340+50)$ times $400 \text{ Hz}$ to get the lower heard frequency, then subtract that value from $400 \text{ Hz}$.
walkthrough: First hearing with stationary train gives the true source frequency $f_s = 400 \text{ Hz}$. Speed of sound is $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and source speed away is $v_s = 50 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
For a source moving directly away from a stationary observer, the observed wavelength is increased and the Doppler equation is $f_o = f_s \times v/(v + v_s)$.
Evaluate the fraction: $340/390 = 0.872$ to 3 s.f., so $f_o = 400 \times 0.872 = 349 \text{ Hz}$ to 3 s.f.
The question asks for the difference: $\Delta f = f_s - f_o = 400 - 349 = 51 \text{ Hz}$.

A.explanation: The observed frequency falls to about $349 \text{ Hz}$, so $400 - 349 = 51 \text{ Hz}$ difference.

B.explanation: This uses the approaching-source denominator $v - v_s$ instead of $v + v_s$ for a source moving away.

C.explanation: This is the new observed frequency of about $349 \text{ Hz}$, not the difference from $400 \text{ Hz}$.

D.explanation: This adds the shift to $400 \text{ Hz}$ as if frequency increased, but a receding source gives a lower frequency.
